analysis.one_liner: Sets national data privacy rules: notice, opt-outs, deletion rights, and FTC enforcement.
analysis.headline: The DATA Privacy Act, a bill to create national data privacy standards, was introduced in November 2023 with no cosponsors and died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that collect data on 50,000 or more people to post clear privacy notices, let people opt out of data collection, get consent before collecting sensitive data like health or precise location, minimize and delete data, and give people access to and the ability to dispute data held about them. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules, and the FTC would get up to 300 new enforcement staff. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, who would gain clear notice of what data companies collect, the right to opt out, deletion and access rights, protection against discriminatory uses of data, and a federal agency and state attorneys general empowered to enforce those rights.

how_it_helps.text: Companies would have to post concise, plain-language privacy notices describing what data they collect, how they use it, and who they share it with [S2].
Individuals could opt out of collection, processing, storage, and disclosure of data linked to them, and could request access to, correction of, or deletion of their data at no charge [S2].

Companies would need affirmative opt-in consent before collecting or disclosing sensitive data such as health, biometric, genetic, or precise location information, and before using data outside the context of the original relationship [S2].

Data practices could not discriminate based on race, sex, gender, sexual orientation, nationality, religion, age, or disability, including discriminatory targeted advertising or price discrimination [S2].
The FTC and state attorneys general could sue violators, with state penalties up to $40,000 per affected individual, and the FTC could hire up to 300 additional enforcement personnel [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large data-collecting companies—data brokers, ad-tech firms, and major online platforms—would bear compliance costs, limits on how they monetize personal data, penalties up to $40,000 per affected individual in state actions, and the cost of hiring privacy protection officers if they exceed $50 million in annual revenue [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and large online platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on an opt-out model: companies could keep collecting data by default and individuals must take action to stop it, which in practice means most people never exercise these rights [S2].
Individuals get no right to sue on their own; enforcement is left entirely to the FTC and state attorneys general, so a person wronged by a violation would depend on government action [S2].

Key standards—what counts as 'reasonable' collection, how discrimination is defined, what security practices are required—are left to FTC regulations to be written over at least a year after enactment, leaving the real rules unknown and subject to future regulatory drift [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give people meaningful, enforceable rights over their personal data at a real cost to the data-driven advertising industry, which is how most 'free' online services monetize users. Its main weaknesses are the default opt-out structure, the absence of any private right of action, and heavy reliance on FTC rulemaking. On balance it would shift power over personal data from companies toward individuals, though imperfectly.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from introduction until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the DATA Privacy Act on November 15, 2023 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day, and no further action was taken [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill was never reported out of committee or voted on [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting, sharing, and selling Americans' personal data are better off because the bill never moved; consumers remain without a national privacy standard beyond the state laws that were already in place.

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and referred it to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-NV)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action—no hearing, markup, or vote—before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or hearings occurred and there were no cosponsors, so no record exists of where parties or members stood.

industries.note: Their business model depends on collecting, combining, and selling personal data, often without meaningful notice. The bill would require consent for sensitive data, allow opt-outs, and expose them to FTC and state enforcement with penalties up to $40,000 per affected individual [S2].

Platforms would face compliance costs, a privacy protection officer requirement above $50 million in revenue, and limits on data monetization, but they also benefit from a federal framework that does not preempt stronger state laws and includes a 'reasonable interest' carve-out for marketing [S2].

industries.industry: Privacy technology and security software firms
industries.note: The bill directs the National Science Foundation to fund research on privacy-enhancing technologies and would drive demand for anti-tracking, encryption, and de-identification tools among covered entities [S2].
Entities handling data on fewer than 50,000 individuals or devices per year are exempt from the core requirements, sparing small firms the compliance burden [S2].
